The 1937–1938 comic strip Torchy Brown, in "Dixie to Harlem" by Jackie Ormes would have been distinctive if only for its heritage—it was almost certainly the first strip to be written and drawn by an African American woman. In 53 weekly episodes, Ormes sketched the experiences of a glamorous heroine who moves from her home in the South to a new life and career at New York's famed Cotton Club.

At first glance, Torchy's adventures might seem as incredible as a fairy tale. The opening panels present a rural Southern community that is nearly idyllic, as Torchy is cared for by a loving aunt and uncle, and freely moves through a pastoral terrain. While journeying to the North, the character is, in the best fairy tale tradition, beleaguered by ominous predators and aided by mysterious helpers. Once in New York, she instantly achieves success as a performer at the Cotton Club, where she mingles comfortably with such African American musical legends as Duke Ellington and Cab Calloway.

Despite the strip's gestures in the direction of the fantastic, Torchy Brown clearly reflects significant cultural concerns. Through her exploration of an entertainer's lifestyle in the almost mythic setting of the Cotton Club, Ormes celebrated and amplified the success of real African Americans who had achieved wide respect for their skill as hardworking and talented professionals. Indeed, so many sequences take place in or around the Cotton Club with Torchy in rehearsal or performance that the Club becomes a symbol for a place where African Americans are measured by what they have to offer, where they are looked upon by a white audience as admirable, instead of being overlooked or looked through. In several episodes, moreover, Ormes explicitly and provocatively likened the artistry of improvisation found in swing music and tap dance with the form of her own comic strip. In the process, Ormes left a record of a moment in the evolution of jazz that also aligned the comic strip, as a mass culture form, with another popular art.

Ormes clearly enjoyed Torchy's triumphs at the Cotton Club, which mirrored her own success as a cartoonist, but she never shied away from the darker possibilities that made Torchy's victories so important. Even during Torchy's "fantastic" journey to New York, the all-too-real world of segregation laws intrudes when Torchy must decide which train car to board. Ormes knew how quickly a newcomer can misread signs and fall into danger. By placing her character in authentic situations where much depends on the courage of the individual, she expanded her social commentary to offer real-life lessons for her audience.
explanation_html:
The opening paragraph does two jobs at once. It introduces the subject, a weekly comic strip of 1937 and 1938 by Jackie Ormes following a young woman named Torchy Brown, and it makes an immediate claim about why that strip matters: it was almost certainly the first written and drawn by an African American woman. Notice the hedge The Author builds in, that the strip would be distinctive if only for that heritage. That construction promises further reasons are coming, so read everything after it as the payoff. The plot summary, South to the Cotton Club in New York, is your map.

Here the passage sets up a problem it will later dissolve. Taken at surface level, Torchy's story looks like pure fantasy: a nearly idyllic rural South with loving guardians and open country to roam, a journey north populated by threatening figures and mysterious helpers, then instant stardom alongside Duke Ellington and Cab Calloway. The paragraph deliberately catalogues fairy-tale machinery, and the hedge that opens it, that this is how things seem at first glance, signals that the catalogue is a reading the passage means to complicate rather than endorse. Keep these specific elements in mind, because the passage names each one precisely.

The pivot arrives with despite. The Author now argues that the fantastic surface sits on top of real cultural work, and three claims stack up. First, by setting so much of the strip in rehearsal and performance, Ormes turned the Cotton Club into a symbol of a place where African Americans were measured by what they could offer and seen as admirable rather than looked past. Second, she drew an explicit parallel between the improvisation of swing music and tap dance and the form of the comic strip itself. Third, that parallel set the comic strip, a mass culture form, beside another popular art. This paragraph carries the passage's core argument.

The closing paragraph blocks an easy misreading of the one before it. Celebration was not the whole story: Ormes also wrote in the darker possibilities that made Torchy's victories matter. The example is concrete. Even inside the supposedly fantastic journey north, segregation law intrudes when Torchy has to choose which train car to board, and the passage notes how quickly a newcomer can misread a sign and fall into danger. Watch the final sentence, because it states the author's verdict: by placing her heroine in authentic situations that turn on individual courage, Ormes widened the strip into social commentary carrying real-life lessons.

Overall structure. The main point is that Torchy Brown deserves attention not only for who made it, almost certainly the first comic strip written and drawn by an African American woman, but for what it did with its material. The Author's purpose is appreciative analysis rather than plot description: the fairy-tale surface catalogued early on is reinterpreted as a vehicle for genuine cultural concerns, including the Cotton Club as a space of earned respect, an explicit link between the strip's form and the improvisation of swing and tap, and a frank treatment of segregation. The structure runs introduction, apparent objection, rebuttal, then qualification, with Ormes's own aims tracked throughout.

The following two passages were adapted from articles published in 2005 and 2002, respectively.

Passage A

There have been two notable efforts to supply credit to self-employed poor people in developing countries. One has been the creation by developing-country governments of state banks, particularly to provide financing to the rural poor. These have mostly been a disaster. The other, much more successful effort involved a number of organizations extending uncollateralized loans to very poor borrowers. One such organization, Bangladesh's Grameen Bank, started in 1976 and soon became famous for its "microcredit" business model.

To qualify, Grameen's customers had to be extremely poor, typically earning less than a dollar a day. To overcome the lack of collateral or data about creditworthiness, customers were required to join small groups whose members monitor each other at weekly meetings, applying varying degrees of pressure to ensure repayment. As loans were repaid, people were allowed to borrow more. The group replaced the security that collateral provides. The model is not perfect, but it does have real virtues and has since spread around the world.

Why did microfinance organizations like Grameen originally limit themselves to providing credit? They assumed that poor people were unable to save and that their sole need was for capital. This assumption, however, was probably faulty at the outset. When BRI, a failing state-controlled rural lender in Indonesia, was transformed into a bank serving poor customers in 1984, it offered not only the usual loan products but also a government-guaranteed savings account with no minimum deposit. This has been an extraordinary success: BRI now has 30 million savings accounts.

Passage B

SafeSave is a financial services provider operating in the slums of Dhaka, Bangladesh. With fewer than 5,500 clients, SafeSave is still a small organization, but it is attracting attention because of its unique products. These products are designed to enable very poor urban residents to turn their capacity to save into usefully large lump sums as conveniently and in as many ways as possible.

In essence, SafeSave offers its clients a full banking service on their doorstep, without asking them to form groups. Bank workers, called collectors, visit each client every day, six days a week. On each visit clients may save, or withdraw, or repay loans in any amount they choose. They may also take loans on their doorstep in values based on their proven capacity to save and repay. Given this flexibility, many clients transact very regularly, in volumes that exceed those of more conventional schemes for poor people. This helps explain why SafeSave's clients tend to pay back loans more quickly than do those of Grameen Bank.

The low interest rate it charges for loans is enough to cover SafeSave's operational costs, in part because of cost-cutting devices such as recruiting collectors from among the urban poor themselves, and full computerization. With growth, SafeSave promises to become fully economically sustainable.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens by sorting attempts to get credit to self-employed poor people into two tracks. Governments in developing countries built state banks aimed mainly at the rural poor, and The Author of Passage A disposes of that track in one verdict: mostly a disaster. The second track, organizations extending small loans without collateral, worked. Bangladesh's Grameen Bank, founded in 1976, is the headline case, and the term to hold onto is microcredit, meaning tiny loans to borrowers no ordinary bank would touch. Notice the frame being built here, a failed government approach set against a successful nongovernmental one.

The second paragraph explains how the successful track actually functions. Grameen's customers had to be extremely poor, and since they had neither collateral nor any credit record, the bank made them join small groups that met weekly and leaned on each other to keep repayments coming; borrow successfully and you could borrow more next time. The key sentence tells you the mechanism: the group replaced the security that collateral provides. The Author of Passage A grades the model carefully rather than celebrating it, calling it imperfect but genuinely valuable, and notes that it has spread worldwide.

Here the passage turns from description to criticism. Why did these lenders offer credit and nothing else? Because The Early Microlenders assumed poor people could not save and needed only capital, an assumption the author judges probably wrong from the start. The evidence is BRI in Indonesia, a government rural lender that was failing until its 1984 transformation into a bank for poor customers, when it added a guaranteed savings account with no minimum deposit alongside its loans. Thirty million accounts later, the demand is hard to deny. Watch that BRI emerges from the very category the first paragraph condemned.

Passage B opens by narrowing the lens to a single organization. SafeSave serves the slums of Dhaka and is tiny, with fewer than 5,500 clients, yet The Author of Passage B presents it as worth attention for the design of its products rather than its size. The stated purpose of those products is to let very poor city dwellers convert their ability to save into lump sums large enough to be useful, as conveniently and in as many ways as possible. Note the change of emphasis: savings is the starting premise here, not an afterthought bolted onto lending.

The middle paragraph shows the operation in practice. SafeSave brings the bank to the doorstep, with collectors calling on every client six days a week, and it requires no groups at all. Clients deposit, withdraw or repay whatever amount they like on any visit, and loan sizes follow from a demonstrated record of saving and repaying. The author then draws a causal line: this flexibility produces unusually frequent, high-volume transacting, which in turn explains why SafeSave's clients repay faster than Grameen's. Mark that explanation, because it rests on an assumption that the two client bases are otherwise comparable.

The closing paragraph answers the obvious practical objection, whether an operation this labor-intensive can pay for itself. SafeSave's low interest rate already covers operating costs, helped by hiring collectors from among the urban poor it serves and by running everything on computers, and The Author of Passage B expects growth to make it fully self-sustaining. This is the only place in either passage where the economics of the provider, as opposed to the experience of the customer, comes under discussion, and it ends the passage on a note of qualified optimism.

Overall structure. Both passages describe financial services that are working for poor people in developing countries, and both arrive at the same underlying point: credit alone is not the whole need. Passage A takes the long historical view, contrasting disastrous state banks with Grameen's group-based microcredit, then arguing that the founding assumption that poor people cannot save was faulty, with BRI's thirty million savings accounts as proof. Passage B narrows to a single small organization, showing in operational detail what flexible doorstep saving and lending looks like in the slums of Dhaka. The relationship is one of scope rather than disagreement: Passage B supplies a working instance of the savings-plus-credit idea Passage A argues for.

Since 1929, cosmologists have known that the universe is expanding. Until recently, they assumed that the expansion is slowing as the universe's own gravity tugs against it. In the late 1990s, astronomers set out to observe the slowing by measuring the distances to exploding stars known as supernovas. To their surprise, the farthest supernovas were much more distant than expected. These findings meant that the expansion of the universe is actually accelerating.

Cosmologists have proposed two explanations for the accelerated expansion of the universe, each one a challenge to the current conception of the universe. The first and more widely accepted theory posits a kind of "dark energy" that causes space itself to stretch. Recent studies of the afterglow of the big bang have bolstered the case for dark energy, suggesting that it might even account for a whopping two thirds of the universe's contents. The simplest version of the dark energy theory postulates that dark energy is an inherent part of the vacuum of space, and that it exerts a constant pressure. The basic notion dates back to 1917, when Einstein proposed such a quantity of pressure, which he labeled the "cosmological constant," in order to explain why the universe is not shrinking under its own gravity. He later abandoned the notion as unnecessary when astronomers found that the universe is in fact expanding, but Einstein's orphaned idea may in fact point to what drives the acceleration.

Some cosmologists postulate that the dark energy that drives the accelerated expansion of the universe is created by a class of "virtual" particles. Particle physicists have known for many decades that, thanks to quantum mechanics, the so-called "vacuum" roils with virtual subatomic particles popping in and out of existence, a process that generates a constant vacuum energy. According to the dark energy theorists, this vacuum energy constitutes the dark energy on which their theory depends. Unfortunately, however, there is a large discrepancy between the predicted value of the vacuum energy and the amount of energy needed to explain the accelerated expansion.

This discrepancy is not an issue for the second theory, as it does not invoke the concept of dark energy at all. Instead, it explains the accelerated expansion of the universe by positing that across very large distances—billions of light-years—gravity no longer works as Einstein's general theory of relativity predicts. Such a change to the theory of gravity would be quite radical, and it would presumably have significant implications for the way gravity works even at short distances. Because these implications could be tested in our own solar system, this might actually be an advantage for the radical theory, since it means that this theory may be easier to test than the dark energy theory.
explanation_html:
The passage opens by laying out a puzzle rather than an argument. Three facts stack up in order: the universe has been known to be expanding since 1929, cosmologists assumed gravity was gradually putting the brakes on that expansion, and astronomers in the late 1990s went looking for exactly that slowdown by measuring distances to exploding stars called supernovas. Distance is the hinge here. The farthest supernovas turned out to sit much farther away than a decelerating universe allows, and the paragraph ends on the reversal that drives everything after it: the expansion is speeding up, not slowing down.

This paragraph announces the structure of the whole passage, then fills in half of it. There are two candidate explanations, and each one strains current physics. The first, and the more widely accepted, belongs to The Dark Energy Theorists, who posit an energy that makes space itself stretch; studies of the big bang's afterglow have strengthened their case, possibly to the point where dark energy is two thirds of everything in the universe. The simplest version treats that energy as inherent in the vacuum, exerting steady pressure, which revives the cosmological constant Einstein invented in 1917 to keep the universe from collapsing and then discarded once expansion was discovered.

Here the passage zooms in on one way of cashing out dark energy, then punctures it. Particle Physicists have long held that empty space is not empty: quantum mechanics has virtual subatomic particles flickering into and out of existence, and that constant churn carries a vacuum energy. The Dark Energy Theorists borrow that energy and identify it as the dark energy their theory requires. Watch the turn signalled by the last sentence. The vacuum energy that physics predicts and the amount needed to produce the observed acceleration are wildly different numbers, so the most natural source for dark energy supplies the wrong quantity.

The final paragraph pivots to the second explanation, and its first words frame that theory by its advantage: it escapes the mismatch that just damaged its rival, because it never invokes dark energy at all. Instead it claims that out at billions of light-years, gravity simply stops behaving the way Einstein's general theory of relativity says it should. The Author concedes that this would be a radical change, since altering gravity at vast scales presumably alters it at short ones too. Then comes the twist: those short-range consequences could be checked in our own solar system, so the wilder theory may be the easier one to test.

Overall structure. The main point is that the surprising discovery of an accelerating universe has produced two competing explanations, and neither one sits comfortably with accepted physics. The Author's purpose is expository rather than advocatory: the opening paragraph establishes the acceleration as an observational surprise, the second and third set out the dark energy theory of The Dark Energy Theorists along with the quantum vacuum energy that Particle Physicists supply for it, and the third paragraph closes by exposing the mismatch in magnitude that account suffers. The fourth paragraph presents the rival proposal that gravity itself breaks down across enormous distances, radical but comparatively easy to test, and the author declines to choose between them.

For most of the past century, scholars in the Anglo-American legal tradition have been skeptical of the view that legal ownership is a matter of possessing any single right. They have advocated the view that ownership is a "bundle of rights" arising from individual judicial decisions in widely diverse cases (e.g., the rights to lease, sell, subdivide, and tax). Accordingly, the concept of ownership per se does not constrain judges' decisions in the resolution of conflicts regarding property use, since the set of rights corresponding to ownership is itself a product of earlier judicial decisions and is open ended. This theory has been criticized by recent proponents of an older view—that ownership is a basic right to exclude others from a particular thing. According to this "boundary theory," appealing, in judicial reasoning, to the right to exclude others is by definition equivalent to appealing to ownership, and so the concept of ownership constrains judicial reasoning.

But while the boundary theory properly recognizes that there is a concept of ownership that constrains legal decisions, it fails to explain crucial features of ownership. Indeed, we might better characterize the view as a theory of nonownership. Its focus is on the position of nonowners, defined in terms of a general duty not to cross the boundaries of objects one does not own. The boundary theory, in effect, relies on a process of elimination to distinguish owners from nonowners: an owner is the last person left after the exclusion of everyone else from the object owned. But this provides only the weakest possible account of the owner's special position: by default the owner is the only one at liberty to use the object after the exclusion of others.

While there is a grain of truth in the boundary theory inasmuch as ownership is an exclusive right, the boundary theory wrongly assumes that what it means for ownership to be exclusive is just that others generally have a duty to exclude themselves from the object owned. However, there is a distinction between a right's being exclusive in the sense that it excludes others from the object of the right and its being exclusive in the sense that its holder occupies a special position that others do not share. A third theory, the "agenda-setting theory," regards ownership as an exclusive right in the second sense but not the first. What it means for ownership to be exclusive is that owners are in a special position to set the agenda for a resource (e.g., farm owners determining the specific uses of their land). The law preserves the exclusivity of ownership not by excluding others, but by harmonizing their interests with the owner's agenda-setting authority. This, rather than the boundary theory's "exclusivity," is the essence of ownership.
explanation_html:
The subject is a dispute about what legal ownership actually is. The Bundle-of-Rights Scholars, dominant in Anglo-American law for about a century, deny that ownership is any one right; it is a collection of rights assembled piecemeal by courts across unrelated cases, such as the rights to lease, sell, subdivide and tax. Their payoff matters: because the bundle is itself built by past rulings and is never closed, invoking ownership cannot settle a property dispute for a judge. The Boundary Theorists, reviving an older position, push back. Ownership is one basic right, the right to exclude others from a thing, so appealing to exclusion just is appealing to ownership, and ownership therefore does constrain judicial reasoning. Notice that the paragraph stages two rivals and takes no side yet.

Here The Author enters, and the target narrows: from this point on the criticism is aimed at the boundary theory, not the bundle view. The concession comes first, that the boundary theorists are right there is a concept of ownership constraining legal decisions. Then the objection: their theory describes nonowners rather than owners. It defines a general duty to stay outside objects you do not own, then identifies the owner by subtraction, as whoever remains once everyone else has been excluded. That subtraction leaves the owner's special position as nothing more than a leftover liberty to use the thing, which the author calls the weakest possible account and the reason the view is better named a theory of nonownership.

The resolution turns on an ambiguity in the word exclusive. The author grants a grain of truth, since ownership really is an exclusive right, then splits the term in two: a right can be exclusive because it keeps others off the object, or exclusive because its holder occupies a special position nobody else shares. The boundary theory reads it the first way. The Agenda-Setting Theory, which the author endorses, takes the second sense and not the first, so the owner's distinctive power is setting the agenda for a resource, as a farm owner decides what the land is used for. The law protects that authority not by fencing others out but by harmonizing their interests with it, and for the author this, rather than exclusion, is the essence of ownership.

Overall structure. The passage argues that the agenda-setting theory captures the essence of legal ownership better than either of its rivals, and the author's purpose is to weigh three competing accounts in order to defend the third. The structure runs in three steps: the opening paragraph stages the standing quarrel between The Bundle-of-Rights Scholars, for whom ownership is an open-ended set of court-made rights that cannot constrain a judge, and The Boundary Theorists, who revive ownership as the single right to exclude; the middle paragraph grants the boundary view its one merit, then charges it with describing nonowners instead of owners; the last distinguishes two senses of exclusive and puts The Author behind agenda-setting authority over a resource as what ownership essentially is.

In France in the early 1790s, the French Revolution, which sought to establish universal individual rights in French society, inspired several arguments for women's rights. Two such arguments, articulated by Marquis de Condorcet and Olympe de Gouges, both active supporters of the Revolution, are especially noteworthy because they constitute radically opposed courses of action in confronting the question of women's rights. Where Condorcet believed that women's rights were a specific instance of rights in general and that these rights would therefore be established through the establishment of universal equal rights, Gouges argued that the political inequalities to which women were subject formed the wellspring of all injustice experienced by women and should therefore be battled through direct political action.

Condorcet, a mathematician and member of the Academy of Sciences with an interest in social equality, did not separate the question of women's rights from the more general one of equal rights for all members of society, believing that all discrimination was an oversight, the result of not reasoning consistently or not fully using one's rationality to guide one's actions. He felt that all people, women and men, were entitled to equal rights because they were thinking, feeling beings, capable of developing moral ideas and reasoning from those ideas. Condorcet thus maintained that women's rights need not be addressed through vigorous political action. Since no reasoning could justify the perpetuation of any inequality, he argued, this intellectually untenable situation of women's inequality was historically condemned to disappear soon.

Where Condorcet's arguments were purely theoretical and did not include specific legislative proposals to end the exclusion of women from politics, the tone and content of Gouges's proposals reflected her objective that women should become politically mobilized in a war against the injustices that she saw men stubbornly perpetuating. Gouges, a writer and an activist for women's rights, exposed harmful inconsistencies in the period's revolutionary universalism, noting that after the Revolution women's political rights were still limited. She believed that women's political inequality was not just another form of inequality but rather the source of women's unequal position in society, and maintained that only the political vigilance of women could prevent men from appropriating the benefits of the Revolution. She argued that the prevailing political inequality kept women at a disadvantage in all their dealings with men, including marriage, and that this ubiquitous disadvantage would continue until women were granted full political rights, equal access to property, and public employment. Gouges, unlike Condorcet, developed her arguments from the details of the inequality that women were experiencing, but unfortunately, even in the atmosphere of the French Revolution, neither's views were widely accepted.
explanation_html:
The opening paragraph sets the stage and then hands you the passage's organizing contrast. The French Revolution's commitment to universal individual rights prompted arguments that women should share in them, and The Author singles out two supporters of the Revolution whose proposed courses of action pull in opposite directions. Condorcet treats women's rights as one instance of rights in general, so securing universal equal rights would secure them automatically. Gouges treats women's political inequality as the source of every other injustice women face, so it has to be fought directly. Read this as a roadmap: the rest of the passage fills in each position in turn.

Now the passage unpacks Condorcet's reasoning. He was a mathematician, and his argument has that flavor: discrimination is not malice but an error, a failure to reason consistently or to follow one's own rationality through. His ground for equal rights is shared capacity, since women and men alike think, feel, and can reason from moral ideas, so any carve-out is simply inconsistent. Notice where that leads strategically. Because no reasoning could justify the inequality, he concludes it is intellectually untenable and will disappear on its own, soon, without vigorous political action. That optimism about timing is doing real work in his position.

The final paragraph turns to Gouges and defines her by contrast. Condorcet's case was purely theoretical, with no legislative proposals; hers is built from the concrete details of what women were actually experiencing, and its tone is combative. She frames the project as a war against injustices men stubbornly perpetuate, and holds that only the political vigilance of women can stop men from appropriating the Revolution's benefits. A writer and activist, she pressed on an inconsistency inside the period's revolutionary universalism: the rhetoric was universal, yet women's political rights stayed limited after the Revolution. Her central claim is causal. Political inequality is the source of women's subordination everywhere, marriage included, so it persists until women hold full political rights, equal access to property, and public employment. The author closes flatly: neither position caught on.

Overall structure. The main point is that the French Revolution's universalism produced two notable but radically opposed strategies for women's rights, and the author's purpose is to lay those strategies side by side rather than endorse either. Structurally the passage is a contrast essay: an opening paragraph that states the opposition, a middle paragraph developing Condorcet's view that discrimination is a failure of consistent reasoning and will therefore disappear without political action, and a long closing paragraph developing Gouges's view that women's political inequality is the root of their subordination and must be attacked directly. The Profiles are The Author, who reports, and Condorcet and Gouges, who disagree about means while agreeing on the goal.

Passage A

In all games, particularly in athletic contests, the central importance of display and representation serves as a reminder of the ancient connections between play, ritual, and drama. The players not only compete, they enact a familiar ceremony that reaffirms common values. Ceremony requires witnesses: enthusiastic spectators conversant with the rules of the performance and its underlying meaning. Far from destroying the value of sports, as some cultural critics have argued, the attendance of spectators is often necessary to a sporting event. Indeed one of the virtues of contemporary sports lies in their resistance to the erosion of standards and their capacity to appeal to a knowledgeable audience. Norman Podhoretz has argued that the sports public remains more discriminating than the public for the arts and that in sports "excellence is relatively uncontroversial as a judgment of performance." The public for sports still consists largely of people who took part in sports during childhood and thus acquired a sense of the game and a capacity to make discriminating judgments.

The same can hardly be said for the audience of an artistic performance, even though amateur musicians, dancers, actors, and painters may still comprise a small nucleus of the audience. Constant experimentation in the arts, in any case, has created so much confusion about standards that the only surviving measure of excellence, for many, is novelty and shock value, which in a jaded time often resides in a work's sheer ugliness or banality. In sport, on the other hand, novelty and rapid shifts of fashion play only a small part in its appeal to a discriminating audience.

Passage B

Hans Gumbrecht argues persuasively that many great moments in sport are beautiful, in the full aesthetic sense of the word. Gumbrecht laments that most contemporary academic analyses of “sport” as a cultural phenomenon tend to be socially patronizing, dismissive of sports fans as having fallen for a modern-day version of the old bread and circus treatment. Such thinkers, he argues, “find it difficult to admit that the fascination with sports can have respectable roots in the realm of aesthetic appeal” more typically associated with the so-called high arts. Conditioned to look for aesthetic pleasure in a concert hall or museum, we fail to recognize that watching a well-played sporting event might be a legitimate aesthetic experience as well.

Gumbrecht grounds his argument in Immanuel Kant's Critique of Judgment. At the center of Kant's writings on aesthetics is his conception of the “beautiful” as paradoxically related to “purposiveness.” The paradox, as recounted by Gumbrecht, is that although “something does not need to have a purpose in order to be beautiful…whatever we find beautiful looks as if it had a purpose.” A triple axel in figure skating or a double play in baseball clearly has no function outside the sport. And yet such actions give a distinct “impression of purposiveness.” They are beautiful to behold because they appear both carefully calibrated and perfectly natural.
explanation_html:
Passage A opens by treating sport as ceremony: games are displays that reenact shared values, and a ceremony needs witnesses who understand the rules. That setup lets The Author of Passage A answer The Cultural Critics, who claim that spectators cheapen sport; on this view spectators are not a corruption but a requirement. The author then adds a stronger claim, that sport has held onto its standards, and enlists Podhoretz to support it, since judgments of athletic excellence remain relatively uncontroversial. Notice the explanation offered for that discrimination: most fans played as children, and playing is what taught them how to judge.

The second paragraph turns the comparison outward to art, and the move is a contrast rather than a new topic. The art audience, the author says, cannot claim the same competence, since only a small core of it consists of amateur practitioners. Relentless experimentation has muddled artistic standards so badly that, for many, novelty and shock are all that is left to measure by, which is how ugliness or banality can pass for achievement. The paragraph closes by swinging back to sport, where fashion counts for little. Hold both halves together: participation breeds judgment, and stable standards follow from it.

Passage B opens on different ground, and its author works as an endorser rather than an independent arguer. The claim belongs to Gumbrecht: great moments in sport are beautiful in the full aesthetic sense, and Passage B calls that case persuasive. The rest of the paragraph identifies his opponents, The Academic Critics, who study sport as a cultural phenomenon while talking down to fans as dupes of bread and circuses. Their blind spot, he argues, is a refusal to grant sport the aesthetic respectability reserved for high art. Trained to find beauty in concert halls and museums, we miss it in a well-played game.

The final paragraph supplies the philosophical machinery. Gumbrecht borrows from Kant, whose work on aesthetics ties beauty to a paradox about purposiveness: a thing need not actually serve a purpose in order to be beautiful, yet whatever we find beautiful looks as though it had one. Applied to sport, the fit is immediate. A triple axel or a double play accomplishes nothing outside its game, so it has no external function, and yet it reads as exactly calibrated and entirely natural. That impression of purposiveness is the whole basis for calling sport a legitimate aesthetic experience.

Overall structure. Both passages set the appraisal of athletic performance beside the appraisal of art, but they travel in different directions and for different ends. The Author of Passage A, backed by Podhoretz, defends sport against The Cultural Critics by arguing that sports audiences, schooled by childhood participation, still judge excellence confidently, while art audiences have surrendered their standards to experimentation and shock value. Passage B reports and endorses Gumbrecht, who draws on Kant's link between beauty and apparent purposiveness to argue, against The Academic Critics, that watching a well-played game can be a genuine aesthetic experience. Both treat sport as unfairly disparaged, but A measures it against art's decline while B asks that it be admitted to art's own category of beauty.

The following passage was adapted from an article published in 1998.

The government of Belize granted concessions for logging on approximately 480,000 acres in its Toledo District. The affected regions are populated primarily by descendants of the Maya, whose civilization flourished throughout Mexico and Central America for hundreds of years prior to European contact. In response, Maya organizations filed a lawsuit challenging the concessions. In the suit the Maya assert rights over lands and resources included in the concessions and seek to have the concessions declared in violation of Mayan rights.

The assertion by the Maya of land and resource rights is based on both common law and international law. Common-law jurisdictions, which derive their common law from English legal tradition, use custom and precedent as bases for deciding court cases, rather than relying solely on written laws or codes. Precedent involves a court's giving weight to analogous cases previously decided by relevant courts. As a former British colony, Belize is a common-law jurisdiction, but courts in Belize have not yet ruled on matters concerning indigenous rights. The argument advanced by the Maya therefore relies substantially on precedents from other common-law jurisdictions, particularly Australia, Canada, and the United States—countries in which courts have recognized indigenous rights based on historical occupancy or use of lands. This approach is consistent with the customary practice of the courts in Belize, which is to look to precedents of other common-law countries in the absence of relevant precedent in Belize's case law.

The common law of indigenous rights is also shaped by norms that are embraced by the world community and that are now part of, or becoming part of, international law. For example, a 1992 decision by the high court of Australia recognizing indigenous rights states that "international law is a legitimate and important influence on the development of the common law, especially when international law declares the existence of universal human rights." Specifically, in recognizing the existence of common-law indigenous rights, the court cited Australia's obligations under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. Belize is also a party to the covenant, and Belize's courts should therefore allow the covenant to inform the creation of common-law rights in Belize.

As a domestic constitutional matter, Belize is free to develop its common-law jurisprudence on the doctrine of indigenous rights independently of other jurisdictions and their incorporation of international norms, regardless of its judicial system's customary practice involving the use of foreign precedent. However, that the common law of Belize flows from the same theoretical origins as that of other jurisdictions that have pronounced in favor of indigenous rights argues for a presumption in favor of recognizing indigenous rights in Belize.
explanation_html:
Start with the facts of the dispute. Belize's government granted logging concessions over roughly 480,000 acres in the Toledo District, and the people living there are largely descendants of the Maya, whose civilization predates European contact in the region. The Maya organizations responded with a lawsuit that does two things: it asserts their own rights over the lands and resources covered by the concessions, and it asks a court to declare the concessions a violation of those rights. This paragraph is pure setup, with no competing viewpoints yet; the legal argument begins in the next one.

Here the passage explains the legal footing of that claim. A common-law jurisdiction decides cases using custom and precedent, meaning earlier analogous rulings, rather than relying only on written codes. Belize, as a former British colony, is one of those jurisdictions, but its own courts have never ruled on indigenous rights, so there is no home-grown precedent to point to. The Maya therefore borrow precedent from Australia, Canada and the United States, where courts have recognized indigenous rights grounded in historical occupancy or use. Notice the closing move: borrowing this way matches what Belizean courts customarily do when local case law runs out.

A second source now joins precedent: norms the world community embraces that are part of, or becoming part of, international law. The example is a 1992 Australian high court ruling that recognized indigenous rights and said outright that international law legitimately influences the development of common law, especially where universal human rights are at stake. That court leaned on Australia's obligations under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. The Author then completes the parallel: Belize is party to the same covenant, so Belizean courts should let it inform the creation of common-law rights there too. Watch that word should, the first place the author argues rather than reports.

The closing paragraph concedes before it concludes. The Author grants that, as a constitutional matter, Belize may develop its own doctrine on indigenous rights however it likes, independent of other jurisdictions and of their absorption of international norms, and even independent of its own habit of consulting foreign precedent. That concession is genuine, and it is why the conclusion lands so modestly. Because Belizean common law flows from the same theoretical origins as the systems that have already ruled for indigenous rights, the author claims only that this argues for a presumption in favor of recognition, not that Belize is obliged to recognize them.

Overall structure. The passage uses the Maya lawsuit over logging concessions in Belize's Toledo District as a case study in how a common-law court should approach a question it has never faced, and The Author's purpose is to argue that the claim rests on sound legal foundations. The structure runs from the facts of the dispute, to the precedents of Australia, Canada and the United States that The Maya invoke, to the international-law layer supplied by the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, and finally to a concession that Belize is free to go its own way. The conclusion is deliberately measured: shared legal origins create a presumption in favor of recognizing indigenous rights, not a requirement.

passage_html:
The success of modern physics has consisted primarily in the analysis of physical reality into its fundamental components. But popular reports that physicists are close to arriving at a "theory of everything" are misleading: such a theory would still be limited to interpreting fundamental interactions and explaining why subatomic particles have the mass, charge, and other characteristics that they do. It would explain "everything" only in the sense that everything is made of particles. It could not predict the behavior of complicated systems like thunderstorms or human beings. Even if one could ascertain the locations and trajectories of all the subatomic particles in such a complicated system, no scientist could compute the behavior of all those particles for any significant time into the future.

The problem of prediction in complicated systems is especially intractable when the system in question is chaotic. The essential characteristic of chaotic systems is that they are "nonlinear." In linear systems, similar causes lead to similar effects, whereas in nonlinear systems the outcome of the process is so sensitive to initial conditions that a minuscule change at the beginning of the process results in a large difference in the end. Consider water flowing out of a faucet. At low velocities the water behaves in a linear fashion, flowing out in a predictable way. But if the faucet is opened wide enough, the water becomes highly turbulent and chaotic, spurting in unpredictable directions. The input is not dramatically different from the input that previously produced a linear result—the faucet is just opened wider—but the result is suddenly very different.

Between the extremes of simple predictability and chaos there can arise behavior that is partly linear and partly chaotic. The emerging science of complexity theory offers promise of explaining the behavior of systems that are on the edge of chaos, in the sense that they retain a degree of order while flirting with chaotic nonlinearity. For example, pockets of turbulence may appear in an otherwise smooth flow, such as when a flowing bathroom faucet suddenly starts rapping loudly. Much of the excitement about complexity theory arises because of the belief that living things are systems of this kind. Cell membranes, for example, are poised on the boundary between a solid and a liquid state and are thus somewhat unstable. Small changes in a cell's local chemistry can produce disproportionately large changes in the cell. While some of these changes are harmful to the cell and may even destroy it, most are compatible with its continued existence and some may even prove biologically useful. Thus, while the cell requires order for its survival, it also needs a degree of disorder to facilitate novelty—development of new structures and behaviors that enable it to cope with changing environmental conditions, and, thus, adapt and evolve.
explanation_html:
The Author opens by granting modern physics its genuine achievement: it has advanced by breaking physical reality down into its smallest pieces. The turn comes immediately. Against Popular Reports announcing an imminent theory of everything, the author argues the phrase oversells what such a theory could do. It would tell you why particles carry the mass and charge they carry and how they interact, and no more; it earns the word everything only on the technicality that everything is built from particles. Notice the concession at the close: even handed perfect knowledge of every particle's position and path, no one could work a thunderstorm or a person forward in time.

This paragraph narrows the prediction problem to its hardest case and defines the term the rest of the passage runs on. Chaotic systems are nonlinear, and the contrast is worth holding onto: in a linear system similar causes produce similar effects, while in a nonlinear one a tiny difference at the start balloons into a huge difference at the end. The faucet does the explanatory work. Barely open, the stream is orderly and predictable; opened wide, the water sprays in directions no one can call. Watch the emphasis in the final sentence: the change in input was small and ordinary, yet the output changed in kind rather than degree.

The final paragraph reaches the passage's real subject by carving out a middle zone between clean predictability and full chaos, where behavior is partly linear and partly chaotic. Complexity theory is the emerging science said to offer promise for systems sitting on that edge, and the author reuses the faucet for continuity: a smooth flow that abruptly starts rapping. Complexity Theorists are excited, the author reports, because living things look like systems of exactly this kind. The cell membrane supplies the example, poised between solid and liquid and unstable enough that small chemical shifts produce outsized effects. Hold onto the closing claim: a cell needs order to survive but also needs some disorder, because disorder is what generates the novelty that lets it adapt and evolve.

Overall structure. The Main Point is that reductive physics, however successful at the level of fundamental particles, cannot predict the behavior of complicated systems, and that complexity theory offers a promising route to explaining the partly ordered, partly chaotic systems lying between predictability and chaos. The Author's Primary Purpose is expository rather than combative: deflate an overstated popular claim, then introduce the science that addresses what that claim leaves out. Structurally the passage moves in three steps, from the limits of a theory of everything, through a definition of nonlinearity anchored by the faucet, to the edge of chaos where Complexity Theorists locate living things, with The Author correcting Popular Reports along the way.
